title: 5 Frog Secrets That Sound Fake. #1 Is a 50-Year Cold Case
description: Frogs that swallow with their eyeballs, hide 89% of their blood in their liver, and break their own bones to make claws. Then the #1 secret: a study (Molecular Ecology, Oct 2026; ScienceDaily 3 Nov) finally used 370+ museum frogs to solve why Brazil's frogs vanished in 1979. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: In 1979, frogs in a Brazilian forest started vanishing. It took 47 years to catch the killer.

scenes.label: Brazil, 1979
scenes.say: Okay, so this happened in one of the richest frog places on Earth. Brazil's Atlantic Forest.

scenes.label: 1979 to 1982
scenes.say: Between 1979 and 1982, whole frog populations at one research station just crashed. And for decades, nobody could prove why.

scenes.label: Saved for #1
scenes.say: The answer was sitting in old museum jars the whole time. And the twist in those jars is number one.

scenes.label: Walking superpowers
scenes.say: But first, you need to know how strange frogs really are. Because frogs are basically walking superpowers.
So today we're counting down five frog secrets that sound fake. Each one is weirder than the last.

scenes.label: Eyes that swallow
scenes.say: Number five. Frogs use their eyeballs to swallow.
Seriously. Next time you see a frog eat, watch its eyes. They blink shut and sink down into its head.
For about a hundred years, people guessed those eyes were pushing the food. But nobody had actually tested it.

scenes.label: Written in 1906
scenes.say: Back in 1906, one writer said a toad's big eyes could press down into its mouth as far as they stick up. Sounds made up, right?

scenes.label: X-ray video, 2004
scenes.say: So in 2004, scientists filmed northern leopard frogs eating crickets. With X-ray video.

scenes.label: Eyes push food
scenes.say: And the X-rays showed it. The eyeballs drop right into the mouth, touch the cricket, and shove it toward the throat.
Then the team stopped the eye muscles from working. The frogs could still swallow, but it got much harder.

scenes.label: 2.3 → 4 swallows
scenes.say: A normal frog needed about 2.3 swallows per cricket. Without eye help, it needed 4. That's 74 percent more work.
Think about that. You use your eyes to find dinner. A frog uses them to push dinner down.

scenes.label: One eye or two
scenes.say: And the eyes don't even have to move together. Sometimes just one eye drops in, depending on where the food sits in the mouth.

scenes.label: The invisible frog
scenes.say: Number four is even stranger. A frog that hides its own blood.

scenes.label: See-through belly
scenes.say: Glass frogs live in Central and South American forests. Flip one over and you can see its heart, its guts, everything.
Here's the problem. Red blood is very easy to see. So how does a see-through animal hide all that red?

scenes.label: Duke + AMNH, 2022
scenes.say: In 2022, scientists at Duke University and the American Museum of Natural History watched glass frogs while they slept.

scenes.label: 89% into the liver
scenes.say: They found that a sleeping glass frog pulls about 89 percent of its red blood cells out of circulation and packs them into its liver.

scenes.label: Liver swells 40%
scenes.say: Its liver even swells by about 40 percent to hold it all. And that liver has a mirror-like coating that hides the red.

scenes.label: 2-3x more see-through
scenes.say: The result? The frog becomes two to three times more transparent while it sleeps. Basically, it turns into a ghost.

scenes.label: 12 hours a day
scenes.say: One of the scientists said these frogs are basically not moving much oxygen around for about 12 hours a day. And they're totally fine.

scenes.label: Wake up, turn visible
scenes.say: When the frog wakes up, the blood rushes back out of the liver, and the frog turns visible again.

scenes.label: No blood clots
scenes.say: And here's the twist. In people, packed blood can form dangerous clots. Glass frogs do this every single day without clotting.
That's why doctors are interested. These tiny frogs might teach us something new about blood clots.
Okay, so far we've had eyes that swallow and blood that disappears. Now things get a little bit Wolverine.

scenes.label: Wolverine frog
scenes.say: Number three. A frog that breaks its own bones to make claws.

scenes.label: Not real hair
scenes.say: Meet the hairy frog from Central Africa. Those hairs are really thin strips of skin that males grow in breeding season.

scenes.label: Cameroon
scenes.say: A Harvard biologist named David Blackburn picked some up in Cameroon. They kicked hard and scratched him until he bled.

scenes.label: Hunters beware
scenes.say: And local hunters in Cameroon know it too. They go to great lengths to avoid touching these frogs while they're alive.
So he studied them in 2008. Inside the back toes, there's a sharp bone held in place by tough tissue.

scenes.label: Bone through skin
scenes.say: When the frog is grabbed, that bone snaps free and punches straight out through the skin of its own toe. Instant claw.

scenes.label: Only claws like it
scenes.say: Cats have claw sheaths. This frog doesn't. Scientists say these are the only animal claws known to cut their way out.

scenes.label: Missed for 100 years
scenes.say: For about a century, scientists who saw the poking bones in museum specimens thought it was just damage from preserving them.

scenes.label: Just 11 species
scenes.say: And out of more than 5,500 known frog species back then, the team found claws like this in only 11.
So yes, it's a frog with secret pop-out claws. But the next frog doesn't need claws at all.

scenes.label: Small but deadly
scenes.say: Number two. The tiny frog that carries enough poison for ten people.

scenes.label: About 5 cm
scenes.say: This is the golden poison frog from Colombia. It's only about five centimeters long. Smaller than your thumb.

scenes.label: 1 frog, 10 people
scenes.say: The American Museum of Natural History says the poison from just one of these frogs could kill ten humans.

scenes.label: Poison darts
scenes.say: Hunters in the Chocó forest rubbed their blowgun darts on its back. Then they let the frog go, unharmed.
Its poison is called batrachotoxin. It stops nerves from sending signals, so the muscles and heart can't keep working.

scenes.label: 2 grains of salt
scenes.say: World Land Trust says an amount of this toxin about as big as two grains of salt could kill a person.

scenes.label: Warning colors
scenes.say: And the bright yellow color? That's a warning sign. It tells predators, eat me and you'll regret it.

scenes.label: Harmless in zoos?
scenes.say: But here's the plot twist. In zoos, golden poison frogs are harmless.

scenes.label: Poison from food
scenes.say: That's because the frog doesn't make the poison from scratch. Scientists think it comes from something in its wild diet, probably certain beetles.
Feed it plain crickets and flies, and the deadliest frog on Earth slowly loses its weapon. You are what you eat, right?

scenes.label: One secret a day
scenes.say: Quick thing. If you like secrets like these, subscribe. I share one wild animal secret every day.
Okay. Superpowers, poison, claws. Frogs seem unbeatable. So what could wipe them out in a forest in Brazil?

scenes.label: The cold case
scenes.say: Number one. The 50-year frog cold case.

scenes.label: Boracéia station
scenes.say: Back in the late 1970s, scientists noticed frogs disappearing across Brazil's Atlantic Forest. At one station called Boracéia, the losses were huge.
Some blamed climate change or extreme weather. But nobody had proof, because the suspect hadn't even been discovered yet.

scenes.label: Chytrid fungus
scenes.say: The suspect was a microscopic fungus called chytrid. It attacks frog skin, and frogs need their skin to breathe and drink.

scenes.label: Named in 1999
scenes.say: Scientists think it came from Asia and spread around the world in the 1970s and 80s. But it wasn't officially described until 1999.
So how do you catch a killer twenty years after the crime? You go to the evidence room. The museum.

scenes.label: Smithsonian jars
scenes.say: A scientist named Ronald Heyer had collected frogs at Boracéia, before and after the die-off. They were stored at the Smithsonian.

scenes.label: 370+ frogs tested
scenes.say: In a study published in October 2026, researchers tested more than 370 of those preserved frogs from 17 species.

scenes.label: 0% → over 50%
scenes.say: The result was stark. Before 1979, zero frogs had the fungus. In the 1980s, more than half of them did.

scenes.label: The global strain
scenes.say: Even better, the fungus found in the first samples after the crash was the global killer strain, the one linked to frog losses around the world.

scenes.label: The missing victims
scenes.say: But here's the creepiest part. The species that crashed the hardest showed no infection at all in the jars.
Why? The scientists think those frogs were so vulnerable that they died before anyone could even collect them.

scenes.label: 501 species, 90 gone
scenes.say: And this wasn't just Brazil. A 2019 global study linked chytrid to declines in at least 501 amphibian species, including 90 presumed extinctions.

scenes.label: Golden toad
scenes.say: Costa Rica's golden toad is one of the species presumed lost.

scenes.label: The comeback
scenes.say: But Boracéia has a hopeful ending. When scientists went back between 2022 and 2024, most species had recovered.

scenes.label: They adapted
scenes.say: The fungus is still there. But the frogs seem to have evolved tolerance. They live with it now.

scenes.label: 5 still missing
scenes.say: Not everyone made it, though. Of the 17 species in those old jars, scientists could only find 12. Five are still missing.
So frogs can swallow with their eyes, hide their blood, and grow bone claws. And still, a tiny fungus almost beat them.

scenes.label: Comment below
scenes.say: Which secret surprised you the most? Tell me in the comments. And should I find out what happened to those five missing frogs?

short.title: Frogs Vanished in 1979. Museum Jars Finally Explain Why
short.description: Brazil's frogs crashed in 1979–82. A Molecular Ecology study (Oct 2026) tested 370+ Smithsonian museum frogs: zero infected before 1979, over half after. Full story on 5 frog secrets on the channel. Part of the Wild Sketchbook.

scenes.say: Nobody solved this frog mystery for 50 years. These old museum jars just did.

scenes.label: Brazil, 1979
scenes.say: In Brazil's Atlantic Forest, whole frog populations crashed between 1979 and 1982. For almost 50 years, nobody could prove why.

scenes.label: Chytrid fungus
scenes.say: The suspect was chytrid, a tiny fungus that attacks frog skin. But it wasn't even named until 1999.

scenes.label: 370+ museum frogs
scenes.say: So scientists opened old Smithsonian jars and tested more than 370 frogs. Before 1979, zero had the fungus. In the 1980s, over half did.

scenes.label: The missing victims
scenes.say: The creepy part? The species that crashed hardest showed no fungus at all. They probably died before anyone could collect them.

scenes.label: 5 still missing
scenes.say: Most species came back, but five are still missing. So why did it take so long? Because nobody solved this frog mystery for 50 years, until now.
